I've always been fascinated by the night sky. As a child, I'd spend hours gazing up at the stars, wondering about the mysteries they held. Now, as an adult, I've taken up astronomy as a hobby. I have a telescope at home, and on clear nights, I can see the craters of the moon, the rings of Saturn, and even the Andromeda Galaxy, our closest neighbor in the cosmos.

But my favorite celestial body is the International Space Station (ISS). It's not a star or a planet, but a human-made marvel orbiting Earth every 92 minutes. I've tracked its path using an app, and there's something magical about seeing that bright, moving dot in the night sky, knowing that it's a laboratory where astronauts live and work.

The ISS is a symbol of human achievement and cooperation. It's a testament to what we can accomplish when we set our minds to it. It's also a reminder that we're all connected, no matter where we are on this pale blue dot. When I see the ISS, I feel a sense of pride and hope. It's a beacon of progress, shining down on us from the final frontier.
